week.t: ISRO: GSLV-F18 places NVS-03, the next-generation NavIC satellite, in orbit
CHAPEA crew leaves NASA’s 3D-printed Mars habitat after 378 days
Earth Observatory: Vega Island’s ice looks like a skull in Landsat 9’s view
Voyager 1: the “Big Bang” power swap and the 18–20 October communications pause
Hubble and Webb release the Cat’s Head Nebula
NUS team wins a Google.org AI-for-science grant

tiles.cap: Overnight, India’s 50 m GSLV put the NVS-03 satellite in orbit. ISRO: “Mission Success!”
tiles.nums: approximate lift-off mass of GSLV-F18, a three-stage rocket about 50 m tall carrying a payload of about 2,250 kg
tiles.p1: GSLV-F18, the 20th flight of India’s Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle, flew from the Second Launch Pad at Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota, late on Friday night; ISRO’s live stream began at 23:20 IST, which is 01:50 on Saturday in Singapore. Early on Saturday ISRO posted: “Mission Success! GSLV-F18 has successfully placed NVS-03 in the intended orbit.” NVS-03 is the third satellite of the next-generation series for NavIC, India’s regional navigation system.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: the satellite carries an indigenous atomic clock alongside procured ones, and adds an L1 signal to the existing L5 and S signals.
deep: The orbit it was aimed at
A geosynchronous transfer orbit: perigee 170 km, apogee 37,023 km, inclination 20.75 degrees, on a launch azimuth of 106 degrees.
Three stages

From ISRO’s brochure: the first stage is the S139 solid motor, 20.1 m long, with four L40H liquid strap-ons; the second stage, GL40HT, is 11.9 m; the third is the CUS15 cryogenic stage, 9.8 m, burning liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen. The payload fairing is 3.4 m across, in its metallic version.
Coverage
NavIC is designed to cover the Indian landmass and a region extending 1500 km around India’s borders.
Where the success line comes from

ISRO’s mission page still read “Launch is planned” when this was written; the success line is ISRO’s own post, made early on Saturday. ISRO captions the photo on this tile “GSLV-F18 on the launch pad”.
tiles.src: ISRO mission page and brochure, 27–28 Oct 2026 · ISRO post, 31 Oct 2026

tiles.cap: From 18 November, a radio message to Voyager 1 will take a full day to arrive
tiles.nums: Voyager 1’s speed (61,155 km/h); it is 16 billion miles (24 billion km) from Earth
tiles.p1: NASA said on Thursday 29 October that engineers had turned off three devices on Voyager 1 and substituted three lower-power alternatives, a swap the team nicknamed the “Big Bang”, done in early September about six weeks after a similar swap on Voyager 2. With their plutonium supply continually depleting, both probes lose about 4 watts of power each year. The mission launched in 1977 with 10 dedicated science instruments; the team had already been forced to turn off two, and without the swap another would have followed as early as summer 2027.
tiles.p2: Also in the report: contact with Voyager 1 was lost on 18 and 19 October during two scheduled contact attempts 24 hours apart, and the signal returned on 20 October. One group of thrusters had gone offline and backups activated automatically, a response known as fault protection. The root cause is still being investigated. Kareem Badaruddin, the Voyager mission manager at JPL, on the signal loss: “We’re relieved to be back in contact with Voyager 1 and are eager to understand what happened.”
deep: One light-day

On 18 November Voyager 1 will be one light-day away: 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion km). NASA: “That means that the radio waves used to communicate with the probe take 24 hours to reach it.” Suzanne Dodd, the Voyager project manager at JPL: “If you want to say ‘hello’ to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response.”
Why swap rather than switch off

The Big Bang was unusual because the three swaps had to happen simultaneously: only by swapping all three could the team both cut the power Voyager 1 uses and make sure heat is properly distributed on the spacecraft.
The farthest thing we have made

NASA calls Voyager 1 the spacecraft that has travelled farther than any other human-made object. The photo on this tile was taken on 27 April 1977 and shows one of the Voyagers in the 25-Foot Space Simulator at JPL, before launch.
Check the arithmetic
Light covers about 300,000 km every second. Multiply by the 86,400 seconds in a day and compare your answer with 25.89 billion km.
tiles.src: NASA JPL, Voyager mission update, 29 Oct 2026

tiles.cap: A ghost cat 7,500 light-years away. Its red eye may be a young star still wrapped in dust
tiles.nums: light-years from Earth to the Carina Nebula, where Hubble and Webb photographed the Cat’s Head
tiles.p1: NASA released the pictures on Thursday 29 October, “just in time for Halloween”: Hubble and the James Webb Space Telescope looked at the same pillar of gas and dust in the Carina Nebula, about 7,500 light-years from Earth, and found a shape like a cat sitting with its back to the viewer. NASA says the cat’s glowing red eye may indicate a young star that is still partially embedded in dust.
tiles.p2: Why it looks like that: the pillar was likely sculpted over time by the intense ultraviolet radiation and winds from massive stars. As that feedback erodes the surrounding gas and dust, the scene changes; NASA calls it a temporary scene that will eventually disperse.
deep: Two telescopes, three views

Hubble’s Wide Field Camera 3 shows an opaque dust pillar edged by a luminous rim of gas. Webb looked at the same pillar with its NIRCam and MIRI cameras. The image processing was by Joseph DePasquale of the Space Telescope Science Institute.
Look for it
The photo on this tile is Hubble’s view. Find the cat first, then the red eye.
A number to picture
Light from this pillar set out 7,500 years ago. What you are looking at is the past.
tiles.credit: Image: NASA, ESA, STScI; processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI)

tiles.cap: Curiosity is firing 150 laser shots into one spot, next to the rock it plans to drill
tiles.nums: Martian days (sols) into Curiosity’s mission when it took this close-up, on 18 October 2026
tiles.p1: NASA’s Curiosity blog for sols 5043 to 5049, posted on Wednesday 28 October by planetary scientist Lucy Lim of NASA Goddard, says that after the Basque Lakes drill campaign the rover has returned to a spot just a few metres away. A block called Chiu Chiu was not a good drill candidate, but the block just beyond it was much more promising; it is now named Nazca, and it is “jam-packed” with disc- and needle-shaped lumps; one leading idea is that the shapes were created as crystals grew. ChemCam is concentrating all 150 of its laser shots on the same spot of a nearby crystal-form-rich target called Toucan.
tiles.p2: Why 150 shots in one place: a normal ChemCam observation is a five-point raster with 30 shots per point. The 150-shot profile should penetrate approximately five times deeper into the rock.
deep: Pictures first

MAHLI, the camera on the arm, takes five overlapping images at slightly different geometries for a Quantitative Relief Model of the surface, and doubles its focus steps for its highest-resolution imaging. The photo on this tile is MAHLI’s close-up of the disc-shaped lumps on Nazca, with scratches from the Dust Removal Tool.
Before the drill

LIBS, the Dust Removal Tool and the APXS spectrometer will all be applied to the Nazca spot before the preload test. The third laser target in the plan, Condor, is a nearby block with a finely layered texture exposed.
Clouds over Mars
Twilight cloud season is beginning, and Curiosity is imaging Phobos, the larger and brighter of Mars’ two moons, at night to estimate the sizes of particles in high-altitude carbon dioxide clouds.
tiles.src: NASA Curiosity mission blog, 28 Oct 2026 (Lucy Lim)

tiles.cap: Landsat spotted a smirking skull in Antarctic ice. The missing snow is the scary part
tiles.nums: glaciers catalogued on Vega Island, east of the Antarctic Peninsula in the Weddell Sea
tiles.p1: NASA Earth Observatory’s image of the day for Friday 30 October shows Vega Island, shrouded in ice in the lonely Weddell Sea, looking like a smirking skull in profile: a nunatak jutting out of the ice forms an eye socket and a lateral moraine forms a mouth. The images were acquired by the Operational Land Imager on Landsat 9 on 22 March 2025 and 10 October 2026; clouds obscured the island in March 2026.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: in the March 2025 image a layer of snow coats the ice, typical of the region’s wettest month. Glaciologist Mauri Pelto of Nichols College: “The winter season was no treat for these glaciers.”
deep: Jawline and eye socket

Pelto on ice exposed to melt: “But when exposed to melt, it weathers away, which will lead to a changing jawline and expanding eye socket.” He added that even a thin cover of new snow from a spring storm would be helpful in the short run.
Four ice caps, 29 glaciers

A paper published in 1982 described the island’s four ice caps and, using early Landsat observations, aerial photos and maps, catalogued 29 glaciers on Vega. Devil’s Bay Glacier has been closely monitored since the austral summer of 1998–1999.
The first visitors
The Swedish Antarctic Expedition of 1901–1903 set out to investigate the geography, geology, climate and wildlife of the eastern Antarctic Peninsula.
Look where it looks
The skull looks toward Devil Island, and Bahía del Diablo (Devil’s Bay) Glacier forms its jawbone.
tiles.credit: Image: NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin

tiles.cap: An NUS team is the only one in Asia among 17 picked for Google.org’s AI-for-science fund
tiles.nums: shared by 17 organisations worldwide under the Google.org Impact Challenge: AI for Science
tiles.p1: NUS announced on Thursday 29 October that Assistant Professor Liu Boxiang and his team from the Department of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences have received a grant under the Google.org Impact Challenge: AI for Science. NUS is among 17 organisations selected globally, and the only one in Asia, to receive a share of US$36 million to advance AI-powered scientific research. The team will use AI to map how genetic variations influence RNA splicing across populations.
tiles.p2: In Liu’s words: “We are at an inflection point where AI is changing the way science is done.”
deep: The question
Everyone’s DNA differs a little. The team wants AI to work out how those differences change RNA splicing, and how that varies from one population to another.
What comes with the money
Recipients also have the option to take part in a six-month Google.org Accelerator.
Why it is on this wall
This is AI being pointed at a hard science question by a team a few MRT stops away, not a chatbot answering questions. Compare it with the Using AI tile.

tiles.cap: Heat is jiggling. Blow on wet skin and the fastest molecules leave, so what is left cools
tiles.nums: one angstrom, a ten-millionth of a millimetre; an atom’s radius is 1 or 2 of them
tiles.p1: The first chapter of Richard Feynman’s Caltech physics lectures, given in 1961–63, starts with a drop of water a quarter of an inch across. Magnified two thousand times, it is forty feet across and still looks like smooth water. Magnified two thousand times again, it is about fifteen miles across and looks like a crowd at a football game seen from a very great distance: molecules, continually jiggling and bouncing. Feynman: “Now the jiggling motion is what we represent as heat: when we increase the temperature, we increase the motion.”
tiles.p2: Try it: wet the back of your hand and blow on it. The molecules that escape are the ones with more energy than average, so the ones left behind have less, and the liquid cools as it evaporates. Feynman: “If we blow on the water so as to maintain a continuous preponderance in the number evaporating, then the water is cooled.”
deep: How small an atom is

Atoms are 1 or 2 × 10⁻⁸ cm in radius; 10⁻⁸ cm is called an angstrom, so atoms are 1 or 2 angstroms in radius. Feynman’s way to remember it: if an apple is magnified to the size of the Earth, the atoms in the apple are approximately the size of the original apple.
Steam

“If we heat the water, the jiggling increases and the volume between the atoms increases, and if the heating continues there comes a time when the pull between the molecules is not enough to hold them together and they do fly apart and become separated from one another.” That is how steam is made.
Brown saw it in 1827

Robert Brown, a botanist, noticed little particles of plant pollen jiggling around in liquid, and found the same motion in water that had been trapped inside an old piece of quartz for millions of years. Feynman works out that the energy of that motion means a speed of a millimetre or so per second for an object a micron or two in diameter.
Temperature now has an exact number

The revised SI, approved in November 2018, defines the kelvin by fixing the Boltzmann constant at exactly 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ joules per kelvin, which ties temperature to energy of motion. Before that, the kelvin was 1/273.16 of the temperature of the triple point of water, 273.16 K.
tiles.src: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. I ch. 1 and 41 · NIST, SI redefinition

tiles.cap: Fire electrons one by one at two slits and, 20 minutes later, they have drawn stripes
tiles.nums: electrons, arriving one at a time, that built the stripes in the 1989 Hitachi experiment; the first 8 looked like random dots
tiles.p1: In 1989 Akira Tonomura and co-workers at Hitachi sent electrons through a double-slit set-up (an electron biprism, which does the job of two slits) at fewer than 1,000 per second and watched them land one by one, detected with almost 100 per cent efficiency. After 8 electrons: scattered dots. After 270, then 2,000, then 60,000, over more than 20 minutes, the dots had built up into stripes, the interference pattern of a wave. In 2002 Physics World readers voted it the most beautiful experiment in physics: 20 votes, more than any other.
tiles.p2: Feynman on this experiment, in his Caltech lectures: it is “impossible, absolutely impossible, to explain in any classical way, and which has in it the heart of quantum mechanics. In reality, it contains the only mystery.”
deep: Bullets, waves, electrons

Feynman sets it up three ways. A machine gun firing at an armour-plate wall with two holes: bullets always arrive in identical lumps and the probabilities just add. Water waves in a shallow trough: the intensity can have any value at all, and the two waves interfere. Electrons from a heated tungsten wire: “The electrons arrive in lumps, like particles,” but “the probability of arrival of these lumps is distributed like the distribution of intensity of a wave.”
Try to watch, and it changes

“By trying to ‘watch’ the electrons we have changed their motions.” Heisenberg’s rule puts a number on it: know an object’s momentum to within Δp and you cannot know its position better than Δx ≥ ħ/2Δp. Feynman: “No one has ever found (or even thought of) a way around the uncertainty principle.”
See the wave yourself, no laser

Exploratorium’s version: two clean new pencils with erasers, one wrapped in a single layer of transparent tape. Hold them together to make a thin slit, hold it about 2.5 cm from your eye and look at a small bright light, a Mini Maglite or a candle flame. You see a line of blobs with dark bands between them: light bending around the edges and interfering. The narrower the slit, the more the light spreads out.
Light plus light equals dark

With a laser pointer shone through two gaps left in a taped-over lice comb onto a card at least 1.5 m away, you get light and dark bands; cover one slit and some of the dark bands vanish. Thomas Young first did this in 1801.
tiles.src: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. III ch. 1 · Physics World, Sept 2002 · Exploratorium Science Snacks

tiles.cap: A gaming PC in a 6-inch cube. One big slow fan keeps it quiet; 4K is where it struggles
tiles.nums: the fan Valve built the Steam Machine around: a cube just large enough to hold it, cooling an AMD CPU and GPU
tiles.p1: Valve’s Steam Machine, in TIME’s Best Inventions of 2026, is a six-inch cube. Valve hardware engineer Yazan Aldehayyat says the team wanted a computer powerful enough to run complex game engines and vivid open worlds but compact enough for a desk or TV stand; making it a six-inch cube just large enough to host a 120 mm fan solved both. That fan cools the AMD CPU and GPU at much lower speeds than a laptop’s, so the Machine is quiet enough for a living room. Inside, per Valve’s store page: a semi-custom AMD Zen 4 processor with 6 cores and 12 threads, a semi-custom RDNA3 graphics chip with 28 compute units, 16 GB of DDR5 memory plus 8 GB of GDDR6 video memory, a 512 GB or 2 TB NVMe SSD, Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.3, running SteamOS 3. Released 22 June 2026 from US$1,049.
tiles.p2: What reviewers found wrong: TechRadar’s Christian Guyton (25 July 2026, 3.33 out of 5) called it “seriously expensive even when compared to full-fat desktop PCs”, found performance “great at 1080p, decent at 1440p, and decidedly mixed at 4K” (Cyberpunk 2077: 71 fps at 1080p Ultra, 17 fps at 4K Ultra), and listed the Steam Controller sold separately, a single USB-C port at the rear, no Wi-Fi 7, games locked to Steam by default, and a small number of crashes.
deep: Why one big fan is quiet

TIME’s explanation: the 120 mm fan cools the CPU and GPU at much lower speeds than those you would typically find in a laptop, which keeps the Machine quiet enough to actually use in a living room. Guyton agreed, calling the fan whisper-quiet.
Two kinds of memory

The 16 GB of DDR5 is the system memory the processor works in; the 8 GB of GDDR6 is video memory for the graphics chip. Guyton wrote that “the ongoing RAM crisis has taken a toll on the Steam Machine’s value proposition”.
Why 4K hurts

A 4K frame has four times the pixels of a 1080p frame, so the same chip has four times as much to draw. Guyton’s table shows it: Shadow of the Tomb Raider 131 fps at 1080p Highest, 47 fps at 4K Highest; Total War: Warhammer III 58 fps at 1080p Ultra, 24 fps at 4K Ultra.
Size and price

15.2 × 16.2 × 15.6 cm and 2.60 kg, with a 17-LED light bar, HDMI 2.0 and one DisplayPort 1.4. You can swap the SSD and the RAM, but that is it. The 2 TB model is US$1,349, and the controller adds US$79.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Kevin Cortez) · Steam store page · TechRadar, 25 Jul 2026 (Christian Guyton)

tiles.cap: A chip configured to be a Nintendo 64, playing the old cartridges in 4K with no lag
tiles.nums: weight of the Analogue 3D, 230 × 180 × 49 mm, with four original-style controller ports
tiles.p1: The Analogue 3D, in TIME’s Best Inventions of 2026, plays original Nintendo 64 cartridges with original controllers but outputs 4K over HDMI. Instead of emulation software it uses an FPGA, a chip whose logic can be configured; Analogue says each of the N64’s three processors (CPU, RSP, RDP) is cycle accurate, executing in parallel at their original speeds, after nearly four years of FPGA engineering. Analogue says the resolution is 10 times the original: the majority of N64 games drew 320 pixels across, some 640.
tiles.p2: What reviewers found wrong: TechRadar’s John-Anthony Disotto (22 November 2025) found no controller and no games in the box, cartridges that sometimes needed a second insertion to register, and warned: “Textures are blurry, controls can feel floaty, and frame rates dip more than you might remember.” His verdict: the N64 at its absolute best, but hard to justify without nostalgia and a cartridge collection.
deep: FPGA versus emulator

An emulator is software on a modern processor imitating the old machine. An FPGA, a field-programmable gate array, has logic that can be configured to behave like the original circuits, running in parallel the way the original did. Analogue’s claim from that: “Lag free, zero signal degradation” and one hundred per cent cartridge compatibility. Disotto found “Everything responds instantly, with no input lag.”
Old TVs, redrawn

It offers Original Display Modes that mimic CRT and PVM tube monitors, and those modes need a 4K-capable display. Disotto called the filters gorgeous and said they help make it the best way to play N64 on a modern TV.
The rest of the box

4K or 1080p output, NTSC and PAL, variable refresh rate, Bluetooth for wireless controllers, dual-band Wi-Fi for over-the-air updates, a 16 GB SD card pre-installed, 48 kHz 16-bit audio, two USB-A ports and USB-C power from a 30 W GaN supply. Region free. Price on Analogue’s store: US$269.99; the review, in November 2025, listed US$249.99. The 8BitDo 64 controller, with a Hall-effect joystick, is US$39.99 extra.
A claim that changed

TIME says the console supports save states; the November 2025 review said they were not available yet. Analogue added them, called Memories, in firmware 1.3.0 on 15 May 2026, so the review, not TIME, is the one that is out of date.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Jessica Sager) · Analogue spec and firmware pages · TechRadar, 22 Nov 2025 (John-Anthony Disotto)

tiles.cap: Make a friend’s face disappear with a hand mirror, leaving only the eyes and mouth
tiles.nums: size of the hand mirror; you also need a white wall and a partner who can sit very still
tiles.p1: Sit so a white wall is on your right and your partner sits a few feet in front of you. Hold the bottom of a hand mirror in your left hand and put its edge against your nose, reflecting surface facing sideways toward the wall, so your right eye sees only the reflection of the wall while your left eye looks forward at your partner’s face. Now move your hand in front of the white surface as if passing a blackboard eraser over it. Parts of your friend’s face disappear.
tiles.p2: Exploratorium’s tips: your friend should sit very still against a plain, light-coloured background, and keep your own head still too. If you cannot see it, switch which eye looks at the wall. Some people need several tries and a few never see it, so don’t give up too soon.
deep: What is going on

Normally your two eyes see very slightly different pictures and your brain combines them into a single three-dimensional image. Here the mirror gives each eye a very different view, and the brain builds a picture that makes sense by selecting bits and pieces from both. It is very sensitive to changes and motion, so it emphasises the moving hand rather than the unmoving face, and parts of the face disappear.
What stays
“No one knows how or why some parts of the face may remain, but the eyes and mouth seem to be the last features to disappear.”
The name
The Cheshire Cat in Lewis Carroll’s 1865 Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland vanishes leaving only its grin. On Halloween, this is your trick.

tiles.cap: Giant sea spiders with 25 cm legs glow for up to 10 minutes, 5,000 metres down
tiles.nums: how far the legs of Colossendeis tasmanica can stretch out from a body roughly the size of a finger
tiles.p1: Science News Explores reported on Friday 30 October that giant sea spiders, retrieved from nearly 5,000 metres below the surface in the Australian Abyss, emit light. Jérôme Mallefet, a marine biologist at the Catholic University of Louvain in Belgium, found them on a 2017 expedition aboard the RV Investigator that hauled up 25,000 specimens in nets. Poking the biggest species, Colossendeis tasmanica, raised a dim light; adding potassium chloride, a salt that can excite bioluminescent cells, triggered them to glow brightly for up to 10 minutes. The glow is described in the October issue of Deep Sea Research Part I.
tiles.p2: They are not true spiders but relatives that split off from a common ancestor on the arthropod family tree some 500 million years ago. Mallefet: “It’s quite impressive for people scared of spiders.”
deep: Where the glow may come from
The legs of giant sea spiders contain the digestive tract, Mallefet says, so the animals might get their glow from the creatures they eat, such as sea anemones, his team suggests.
Most of the deep sea glows

Some 76 per cent of deep-sea creatures produce a clear glow, a trait called bioluminescence that dates back 540 million years. A report from more than a century ago described a sea spider that “shone like a star, all its legs being lit along their surface with a strange blue radiance.”
Glow versus fluorescence

Three sea-spider species also glowed green when Mallefet shone ultraviolet and blue light on them. That is fluorescence: absorbing light of one wavelength and re-emitting it as another. Mallefet is not sure what value the sea spiders get from it.
tiles.src: Science News Explores, 30 Oct 2026 (Joshua Rapp Learn)

tiles.cap: The students who got their answers from AI scored 17% worse on the test
tiles.nums: on the exam, after working with a chatbot
tiles.p1: Nearly 1,000 high-school maths students in Turkey were split three ways: problem sets with a plain ChatGPT-style bot, with a version that only gave hints, or with books and notes. While the bot was there the chatbot group looked brilliant, 48% more problems right. Then the AI was taken away for the exam. They scored 17% below the students who never had it.
tiles.p2: Why: they had the answers without doing the thinking, so nothing stuck.
deep: The hint-only version was different
Students who used the tutor that refused to give answers did 127% better in the sessions and then matched the book group on the exam. Same technology, different design, opposite result.
What the researchers concluded
The problem was not AI. It was asking for the answer instead of asking for help. Hamsa Bastani, one of the authors, called the result a cautionary tale.
Try it on yourself
Next hard problem, ask only for a hint, then close the chat and finish alone. See whether you still remember it a week later. This includes the maths set-up your dad built with Claude.

tiles.cap: Artemis III’s 212-foot core stage now stands between its two boosters
tiles.nums: height of the SLS core stage now stacked between its boosters, about 65 metres
tiles.p1: NASA said on Wednesday 28 October that technicians at its Kennedy Space Center in Florida had lifted the Artemis III SLS core stage out of High Bay 2 of the Vehicle Assembly Building and set it between the twin solid rocket boosters in High Bay 3. The 212-foot stage (about 65 metres) hung from a one-of-a-kind lifting beam designed to place it onto the mobile launcher. NASA’s photos of the move and the stacking are dated Thursday 22 to Sunday 25 October, when a caption says the short stack was complete.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: this is the rocket that will carry Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio, Andre Douglas and ESA’s Luca Parmitano on the Earth-orbit docking rehearsal described in the Artemis III tile.
deep: What comes next

Once testing and checkouts are complete, the core stage and booster stack rolls out to Launch Pad 39B for a tanking test: liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen will be loaded only into the core stage, and the launch teams will run through their countdown procedures and timelines. The page gives no rollout date; NASA’s Artemis III mission page says the flight is launching in 2027.
Four engines
One of NASA’s photos, from 22 October, shows the four engines at the base of the stage, each covered in a red cap.
The mission
Artemis III will carry four astronauts in Orion atop SLS to test rendezvous and docking between Orion and commercial spacecraft from Blue Origin and SpaceX, ahead of future crewed Moon landings.

tiles.cap: Four people walk out of a fake Mars on Saturday after 378 days inside
tiles.nums: days of isolation in a 3D-printed habitat at NASA’s Johnson Space Center, Houston
tiles.p1: On Saturday 31 October, Ross Elder, Ellen Ellis, James Spicer and Matthew Montgomery leave the 1,700-square-foot, 3D-printed habitat at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston where they have lived since 19 October 2025. The CHAPEA Mission 2 crew spent 378 days simulating a Mars mission: simulated spacewalks, habitat maintenance and growing plants, with communication delays, limited resources and isolation thrown in.
tiles.p2: NASA streams the exit ceremony live from 3 p.m. EDT on Saturday, which is 3 a.m. on Sunday in Singapore.
deep: What the data is for
NASA says the mission’s data could help plan lunar missions: food system design, how crews use their time, Deep Space Network bandwidth, and medical and behavioural support.
Who is there
Johnson Space Center director Vanessa Wyche and NASA astronaut Jack Hathaway will give remarks at the ceremony.
A thought to test
378 days is longer than a year: the crew went in before last Halloween and come out the day of this one.

tiles.cap: Woodlands hit 36.1 °C on 23 October. Now the winds go slack, and the haze should ease
tiles.nums: highest daily maximum of the fortnight, recorded at Woodlands on 23 October 2026
tiles.p1: The Meteorological Service Singapore said on Thursday 29 October that the Southwest Monsoon is weakening and inter-monsoon conditions are setting in. The second half of October brought winds mostly from the southeast or southwest, which carried smoke haze to Singapore: air quality reached Unhealthy levels on seven days and Very Unhealthy on three between 16 and 28 October. The inter-monsoon period brings light and variable winds instead, so smoke haze is less likely to reach Singapore and the haze situation is expected to improve.
tiles.p2: Also in the review: daily maximums above 34 °C on most days, and most of the island had below-average rain. Tanjong Katong was 72 per cent below average while Punggol was 24 per cent above.
deep: The first half of November

Moderate to heavy thundery showers in the afternoon on most days, sometimes into the evening; total rainfall forecast slightly above average; daily maximums between 33 and 35 °C on most days, with a few days slightly above 35.
The wettest spot
The highest daily rainfall of the fortnight was 81.0 mm at Tuas South on 21 October.
Across the water

NEA’s regional page on Thursday evening: scattered hotspots mainly in southern Kalimantan, moderate to dense smoke plumes over southern and eastern Kalimantan, and a few air quality stations in Sumatra and Kalimantan reporting Unhealthy levels. Extensive cloud cover hid the full picture.
Yesterday’s forecast
NEA’s PSI forecast for Thursday 29 October was 60 to 90, Moderate. At 5 pm on Wednesday the 24-hour PSI was 66 to 78.
